title: 1920, April 6 two spans and a pier were taken out by an ice flood
description: On April 5, long-awaited renovations to the bridge were finally completed after years of weather damage and strain from log drivers had left it in disrepair. The repairs were much needed, as the wooden structure was weak and overdue for an overhaul. However, just as the bridge was ready to reopen, disaster struck. A night of heavy rain caused water levels to rise and ice to break up, a perfect storm. Normally, ice would flow down the eastern shore, but on April 6, 1920, it swept unexpectedly down the western side, destroying two spans and a pier. Once again, the town faced a devastating setback. (Photo courtesy of Hazel Palmer) A vivid account from a newspaper clipping dated April 22, 1920, captures the drama of that day. Kenneth Cox, who would later serve in World War II, was on his way with his father to cut wood for Arthur Baird when the bridge gave way. They lived on the west side of the river and had just reached the bridge approach when Henry Ginson, returning home after delivering milk, raced his horse off the shaking bridge as ice gnawed away at the pier below. Frank “Long” Shaw, running toward the western end, shouted to the Coxes, "Stay off, stay off! She's going to go any minute!" And she did. As “Long” Shaw set foot on solid ground, the bridge collapsed behind him, timbers tumbling into the river, and in moments, Hartland’s vital link was lost. (Henry Ginson was Ward Ginson’s father)
